chunks: And with the first chain of narration, from Ali ibn Mahziyar, [from al-Hasan ibn Ali ibn Faddhal,] from Ali ibn Uqba, from Jarud ibn al-Mundhir, he said: I heard Abu Abdillah Ja‘far ibn Muhammad, upon them both be peace, saying:

The most difficult of deeds are three: your being just to the people from yourself, until you are not pleased for yourself with anything from them except that you are pleased for them from yourself the like of it; and your sharing with the brother in wealth;

and the remembrance of Allah in every situation. [And] it is not that you say: glory be to Allah, and praise be to Allah, and there is no god except Allah, and Allah is the greatest, only; but rather, when there comes upon you something that Allah has forbidden from it, you abandon it.

key_terms.إنصاف: Equity/fairness toward others; treating people as you would wish to be treated
key_terms.الأعمال: Deeds/actions; the ethical acts that define true faith
key_terms.ذكر الله: Remembrance of Allah; here redefined beyond verbal recitation to include moral conduct
key_terms.سبحان الله: Glory be to Allah; a common formula of verbal dhikr
key_terms.مؤاساة: Sharing and solidarity; specifically sharing one’s wealth with fellow believers

ai.seo_question: What are the three most difficult deeds according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: In this narration from al-Amali of al-Mufid, Imam Ja‘far al-Sadiq (a.s.) identifies the three most difficult deeds for a believer: (1) treating people with the same fairness you expect for yourself, so that you accept nothing from them unless you would give them the equivalent; (2) sharing your wealth with your brother in faith; and (3) remembering Allah in every situation—not merely by uttering phrases like Subhanallah and Alhamdulillah, but by actively abandoning whatever Allah has forbidden whenever it presents itself. This teaching, addressed to the early Shia community in Kufa and Medina, redefines dhikr (remembrance of God) as ethical action rather than verbal recitation alone, reflecting the Imam’s emphasis on practical piety over ritualistic formalism.
